lesson.title: The Capacitance You Never Asked For
lesson.summary: Real components and wires have unavoidable capacitance between any two conductors separated by an insulator, and this parasitic capacitance can quietly reshape how a circuit behaves at high frequency.
lesson.body:
Every capacitor you have studied so far was drawn deliberately: two plates, a dielectric, a known value of C. But capacitance is not a feature you have to design in. It is a geometric fact about any two conductors separated by an insulator, and it appears whenever two pieces of metal sit near each other with a voltage difference between them, whether you wanted a capacitor there or not. Two adjacent traces on a circuit board, the two leads of a resistor, the windings of a coil, even your finger near a sensitive input, all form tiny unintended capacitors called parasitic capacitance.

Recall that an ideal resistor has one property, resistance, and nothing else. An ideal wire has zero impedance at any frequency. Real components fall short of these ideals in a specific, physical way: the packaging, leads, and internal geometry of a real part put conductors close together, and Q equals C times V tells us that any such pair, held at different potentials, stores charge. That stored charge is a capacitance, typically a few picofarads to a few tens of picofarads for small components, small enough to ignore at DC and audio frequencies but not always negligible as frequency climbs.

The reason parasitic capacitance matters is frequency dependence. A capacitor's opposition to current, its reactance, is Xc = 1/(2*pi*f*C). At low frequency, Xc for a few picofarads is enormous, megohms or more, so the parasitic path carries essentially no current and the component behaves as advertised. As frequency rises, Xc falls, and eventually the parasitic capacitance offers a lower impedance path than the component itself, quietly bypassing it.

Consider a wirewound resistor rated at R = 10 k ohms, whose winding geometry produces a parasitic capacitance of about Cp = 5 pF across its terminals. The frequency at which this parasitic path becomes comparable to the resistor itself is found by setting Xc equal to R: f = 1/(2*pi*R*Cp). Plugging in, R*Cp = 10,000 ohms times 5e-12 F, which is 5e-8 seconds. Then f = 1/(2*pi*5e-8) = 1/(3.1416e-7), which works out to about 3.18 MHz. Below a few hundred kHz this resistor behaves like a clean 10 k ohm resistance. By 3.18 MHz, the parasitic capacitance is carrying as much signal as the resistor, and above that the part starts looking capacitive rather than resistive.

This is why circuit designers cannot treat datasheet values as the whole story once frequency enters the megahertz range. Keeping traces short and well separated, choosing resistor styles with lower winding capacitance for RF work, and adding guard traces are all direct responses to parasitic capacitance. It is also the first crack in the real versus ideal picture: an ideal resistor has no frequency limit, but every real one eventually stops being a resistor and starts being a capacitor in disguise.
